title: Review: Catalysis (homogeneous and heterogeneous); Enthalpies of solution and hydration; Calorimetry; Standard enthalpies of formation and combustion; Hess's law cycles
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EN02#t2 term and clue written for the game; EN05#t2 term and clue written for the game; KN08#t2 term and clue written for the game; EN07#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN02#N.13, EN04#N.4b, EN05#N.8b, EN07#N.13, KN08#N.14, EN02#N.5b, EN04#N.9b, EN05#N.3b, EN02#N.11b, EN04#N.10, EN05#N.12. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Polystyrene cup
items.clue: With a lid, stirrer and thermometer, it holds two solutions while they react.

items.label: Enthalpy of formation
items.clue: ΔH when exactly 1 mol of a compound is made from its elements; zero for an element.

items.label: Activation energy
items.clue: The barrier to reaction, which is lower along the different route; ΔH stays the same.

items.label: Endothermic
items.clue: Dissolving of this kind makes the water colder: more energy is absorbed than released.

questions.stem: A student measures the enthalpy change when potassium chloride dissolves in water. The temperature falls. The student uses a thin glass beaker with no lid instead of an insulated cup. How does the student's value of ΔH compare with the accepted value?

options.text: Less positive: energy flows in from the warmer room, so the fall in temperature is too small.
More positive: heat escapes from the solution to the room, so the fall in temperature is too big.
Less positive: the glass gives out cold to the room, so the fall in temperature is too small.
The same: ΔH depends only on the amount of KCl dissolved, not on the container.

questions.stem: A process occurs in two steps. Step 1, A → B, is slow and has ΔH₁ = +30 kJ/mol_rxn. Step 2, B → C, is fast and has ΔH₂ = −80 kJ/mol_rxn. Which of the following gives the correct ΔH for the overall process A → C, with a valid justification?

options.text: +30 kJ/mol_rxn, because the slow step controls the overall energy change
+50 kJ/mol_rxn, because energy released by a process is counted as positive
−50 kJ/mol_rxn, because energy is conserved, so the ΔH values of the steps add
−110 kJ/mol_rxn, because energy taken in by step 1 is given out again in step 2

questions.explanation: ΔH = +30 + (−80) = −50 kJ/mol_rxn. The speed of each step does not affect ΔH.

questions.stem: Methane burns: CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l). ΔH°f (kJ/mol): CH₄(g) −74.8, CO₂(g) −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8. What quantity of heat is released when 0.500 mol of O₂(g) is consumed by this reaction at standard conditions?
A student stirs potassium nitrate, KNO₃, into water in an insulated cup. The temperature falls from 21.0 °C to 14.5 °C. Which statement explains the fall?

options.text: Water molecules surrounding the ions absorb energy from the water, cooling it.
Separating the ions releases energy, but not enough to warm the water.
Separating the ions absorbs more energy than ion–water attractions release.
The dissolving salt releases energy to the water, which lowers its temperature.

questions.explanation: The energy to break up the solid outweighs the energy released by the new ion–water attractions. The difference is taken from the water, so it cools: dissolving KNO₃ is endothermic.

questions.stem: High in the atmosphere, chlorine atoms destroy ozone in two steps. Overall: O₃ + O → 2O₂. Which statement is correct? Step 1: Cl + O₃ → ClO + O₂. Step 2: ClO + O → Cl + O₂.

options.text: ClO is the catalyst, as it is formed in one step and used up in the next.
O₃ is the catalyst, as it reacts in the first step.
Cl and ClO are both catalysts, as neither appears in the overall equation.
Cl is the catalyst and ClO is an intermediate.

questions.explanation: Cl joins in, changes to ClO, then comes back as Cl, ready to go round again.

questions.stem: When 10.0 g of solid X dissolves in 40.0 g of water at 21.0°C in an insulated calorimeter, the dissolution releases 1.67 kJ of energy. Assume that the specific heat capacity of the solution is 4.18 J/(g·°C) and that no energy is lost from the calorimeter. What is the final temperature of the solution?
questions.explanation: ΔT = 1670 J ÷ (50.0 g × 4.18 J/(g·°C)) = 7.99°C, so the final temperature is 21.0 + 7.99 = 29.0°C.

questions.stem: The enthalpy changes of these reactions are known: S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g), ΔH₁; 2 S(s) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g), ΔH₂. The enthalpy change of 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g) can be written as ΔH = ΔH₂ + nΔH₁. What is the value of n?
questions.explanation: Reverse the first equation (sign changes) and multiply by 2. ΔH = ΔH₂ − 2ΔH₁, so n = −2.

questions.stem: For which of the following equations is the standard enthalpy change, ΔH°, equal to the standard enthalpy of formation of CaO(s)?
questions.explanation: One mole of CaO(s) forms from its elements in their standard states. The ½ keeps exactly one mole of product.

questions.stem: A spirit burner containing ethanol, C₂H₅OH, heats 150.0 g of water in a copper can. Burning 0.920 g of ethanol raises the water's temperature from 19.0°C to 40.5°C. c(water) = 4.18 J/(g·°C); molar mass of ethanol 46.08 g/mol. What ΔH for the combustion of ethanol do these results give?

Graphite turns into diamond only at enormous pressures, so ΔH for C(s, graphite) → C(s, diamond) can't be measured directly. But both forms burn. (1) C(s, graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −393.5 kJ/mol_rxn · (2) C(s, diamond) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −395.4 kJ/mol_rxn. What is ΔH° for graphite → diamond?
questions.explanation: Keep (1); reverse (2), so its ΔH becomes +395.4. Add: CO₂ and O₂ cancel. ΔH = −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Propane can't be made cleanly from carbon and hydrogen. These reactions can be measured in a calorimeter: (1) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH° = −393.5 kJ/mol_rxn · (2) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH° = −285.8 kJ/mol_rxn · (3) C₃H₈(g) + 5O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l), ΔH° = −2219.2 kJ/mol_rxn. What is ΔH°f of propane, for 3C(s) + 4H₂(g) → C₃H₈(g)?
